v.why: At high learning rates many runs are diverged or near chance, so alpha's usual harm is compressed toward zero and L2 may even help by bounding weight growth.
Under standard parameterisation the function-space change per Adam step grows with fan-in, so widening pushes an already-large learning rate past stability.
High-variance tiny-batch gradients compound through an extra layer, destabilising deeper nets more than shallow ones.
Strong L2 shrinks every weight matrix, so an extra layer multiplies another shrunken factor into the end-to-end map and deepens underfitting.
With a tiny learning rate the net is already undertrained in 243 epochs, so cutting the number of updates via a larger batch hurts much more.
Large batches give few, low-variance updates, so a larger learning rate restores progress without the instability it causes at small batch.
In a one-hidden-layer net width is the only route to capacity, whereas deeper nets already get capacity from depth, so extra width matters more when shallow.
In sklearn MLPs the L2 gradient is divided by the batch size and applied fewer times per epoch, so large batches dilute the extra penalty.
When strong L2 forces underfitting, extra units restore capacity the penalty removed, so widening helps more under heavy regularisation.
At large learning rates deeper nets diverge or suffer dead-ReLU collapse sooner, so adding a layer is more harmful there.
